title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells
authors: Kentaro Nakajo, Hojun Im, Keiichiro Nishimura, Masahiro Teraoka, Masaya Kikuchi
abstract: While graphene/n-type silicon (Gr/n-Si) and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si solar cells offer a cost-effective alternative to conventional photovoltaics, achieving simultaneous high power conversion efficiency (PCE) and long-term environmental stability remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report the synergistic enhancement of both performance and stability in a planar trilayer PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si Schottky junction architecture. By systematically benchmarking this hybrid device against pristine Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells fabricated on untextured substrates, we isolate the fundamental optoelectronic and barrier functions of the carbon lattice. Comprehensive analyses reveal that the PEDOT:PSS layer simultaneously functions as an anti-reflection coating, a moderate p-type dopant for the underlying graphene, and a conductivity enhancer, collectively optimizing interfacial charge transport. Consequently, the trilayer device achieves a PCE of 8.52%, markedly outperforming the pristine Gr/n-Si reference cell (4.56%). Crucially, the atomic impermeability of the graphene sheet serves as a robust environmental barrier. While bare PEDOT:PSS/n-Si junctions retained only ~29% of their initial efficiency after 75 days of ambient exposure, graphene shields the active junction from moisture-induced degradation of the hygroscopic PEDOT:PSS overlayer. This enables the trilayer device to retain approximately 90% of its initial efficiency over the same 75-day period. The complementary roles of graphene as both a highly crystalline charge transport interface and an impermeable protective barrier establish a highly effective strategy for engineering high-efficiency, environmentally stable hybrid photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: A PEDOT:PSS/graphene/n-Si trilayer creates a synergistic Schottky junction that boosts both power conversion efficiency and long-term stability compared with single-layer graphene or PEDOT:PSS devices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The design shows how a thin carbon-based interlayer can simultaneously tune interfacial optics, carrier transport, and environmental protection in low-cost silicon photovoltaics.
method: Built a planar PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si trilayer and compared it with Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells.
Used PEDOT:PSS as an anti-reflection layer, mild p-dopant for graphene, and conductivity enhancer.
Evaluated device performance and aging under 75 days of ambient exposure on untextured substrates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The trilayer reached 8.52% PCE versus 4.56% for pristine Gr/n-Si, and retained about 90% of its initial efficiency after 75 days, while PEDOT:PSS/n-Si retained only ~29%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was demonstrated on untextured laboratory substrates, so scalability, surface-texture compatibility, and fabrication reproducibility still need validation.
infographic.paper_title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells

title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Sofiia Kosar, Anil R. Pininti, Vladyslav Hnapovskyi, José P. Jurado, Subhashri Mannar, Lorenzo Mardegan
abstract: The scalable fabrication of high-quality, large-area perovskite thin films is hindered by microscopic inhomogeneities, particularly residual compositional impurities formed during processing. Identifying these impurities, understanding their impact on device operation, and enabling their rapid detection are essential for upscaling perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Here, nano-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy combined with high-resolution optical and scanning probe techniques was used to identify detrimental impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films relevant to tandem solar cells. Photo-stress experiments revealed that degradation of the perovskite layer initiates at impurity-perovskite interfaces, demonstrating that impurities act as failure nucleation sites. Leveraging these insights, a rapid, non-invasive, and high-throughput framework based on high-resolution reflected light microscopy and machine learning-supported image analysis was developed, enabling detection and quantification of harmful impurities in as-prepared films within seconds. Films with higher impurity density show accelerated early degradation, establishing this parameter as an early-warning metric for stability screening. Extending this framework to degradation tracking further reveals coupled photo- and thermo-chemical contributions to impurity-mediated instability. Overall, this work establishes a practical chemically-validated diagnostic imaging framework for rapid pre-screening of perovskite films to enable stable and scalable PSCs.

infographic.key_insight: Microscopic residual impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films act as degradation nucleation sites, and they can be rapidly detected with microscopy plus machine learning before devices fail.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast, non-invasive pre-screening of perovskite films to flag stability risk early, supporting scalable manufacturing of more durable solar cells.
method: Nano-FTIR to chemically identify impurity compositions
High-resolution reflected-light microscopy to image impurity distributions
Machine learning-assisted image analysis for seconds-level impurity detection
infographic.evidence_signal: Photo-stress and degradation-tracking experiments showed that higher impurity density correlates with faster early degradation and that failure starts at impurity–perovskite interfaces.
infographic.watch_item: The diagnostic framework is chemically validated for the studied film system, but transfer to other perovskite compositions and manufacturing conditions will need re-calibration.
infographic.paper_title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells are typically evaluated using random data splits, which we show systematically leak information through massive internal duplication. Because nearly two-thirds of curated devices share their exact recipe with another, random splits primarily reward the mere recall of historical data rather than testing true physical generalisation. To solve this, we mapped the institutional provenance of the Perovskite Database and established a rigorous hierarchy of grouped splits that progressively isolate duplicate devices, publications, and institutions. Benchmarking thirteen models establishes new state-of-the-art performance across all splits and reveals a critical regime shift: while tree ensembles dominate random splits by recognising familiar recipes, their ranking collapses on genuinely unseen institutions and future discoveries, where composition-aware neural architectures excel. Furthermore, feature importance demonstrates that the device architecture and fabrication methodology dictate final efficiency just as strongly as the absorber chemistry. This standardised protocol empowers the community to separate memorisation from true physical discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Random train/test splits in perovskite-ML benchmarks can drastically overestimate performance because duplicated recipes leak information, so provenance-grouped evaluation is needed to measure true generalisation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For device optimization, this protocol helps researchers choose models and claims that transfer to genuinely new perovskite chemistries, fabrication routes, and institutions rather than to familiar historical records.
method: Mapped institutional provenance in the Perovskite Database.
Built a hierarchy of grouped splits to isolate duplicates, publications, and institutions.
Benchmarked 13 models across increasingly strict evaluation settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that nearly two-thirds of curated devices share their exact recipe with another, and that model rankings shift sharply when moving from random splits to unseen institutions and future-discovery splits.
infographic.watch_item: Grouped evaluation is more realistic but may reduce apparent scores and requires careful provenance tracking, especially when metadata are incomplete or inconsistently recorded.
infographic.paper_title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics

title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.

infographic.key_insight: V-PaSS improves perovskite solar-cell prediction by encoding absorber alloys and device stacks with physics-aware, semantically rich representations instead of treating them as fixed categorical inputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes extrapolative screening more reliable for new perovskite compositions, unfamiliar transport layers, and previously unseen laboratory settings.
method: Interpolates relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure ABX3 endmembers using Vegard’s law plus learned bandgap bowing to model mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers.
Encodes device architecture with layer order, polarity (n-i-p vs p-i-n), interfacial band offsets, and chemical text via a scientific language model.
Combines these features with tree-ensemble models for property prediction under an institution-grouped evaluation protocol.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under unseen-laboratory testing, V-PaSS achieved 2.861% MAE, outperforming a gradient-boosted baseline (3.017%) and the best tuned benchmark (2.912%), with especially strong gains on unseen alloys and transport layers.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the availability and quality of endpoint crystal graphs, band-offset information, and reliable chemistry metadata, which may limit transfer to poorly characterized materials.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells

title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting
authors: Jelena Simeunović, Baptiste Schubnel, Pierre-Jean Alet, Pascal Frossard, Rafael E. Carrillo
abstract: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.

infographic.key_insight: PING uses physics-informed graph learning to forecast advection-diffusion dynamics on irregular sensor networks, improving cloud-motion and solar power prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can help grid operators and PV plants better anticipate intra-day solar output by combining satellite cloud information with ground-based measurements.
method: Models advection-diffusion as signals on a graph for irregular spatial grids
Adds a discretized physics constraint as a soft loss term to keep predictions physically consistent
Uses the learned forecasts as input to a hybrid PV power prediction pipeline
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports performance on synthetic and real datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index data, with results on par with state-of-the-art models and improved PV forecasting when coupled to sensor and satellite data.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the quality and coverage of irregular sensor and satellite data, and the physics loss must be balanced carefully to avoid over-constraining learning.
infographic.paper_title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting

title: Device Model Linking Singlet and Triplet Spin-State Properties to Organic Photovoltaic Device Characteristics
authors: Jun Du, Liming Liu, Jun Yan
abstract: This work proposes an exciton-kinetics coupled drift-diffusion (EKDD) model that bridges device-level charge transport with singlet and triplet excited-state kinetics. State populations and reversible photophysical transitions are solved self-consistently, enabling transient and steady-state device response calculations. We investigate how LE-CT, CT-CS, and LE-T energy offsets, together with triplet-transfer kinetics, govern charge generation, recombination, voltage loss, and extraction in organic photovoltaics. We identify CT-CS offset as a primary, largely overlooked factor controlling charge generation and voltage loss. A positive offset makes CT3-CS separation exothermic and improves generation, but lowers CS energy and increases voltage loss; a negative offset makes separation endothermic and highly temperature-sensitive. The model reproduces triplet-mediated recombination in PM6:Y6 and material-dependent triplet recycling in D18:NFA blends. We propose design rules for balanced generation and voltage loss via two charge-transfer channels: the LE-CT-CS pathway favors a moderate LE-CT offset of about 0.15-0.20 eV and a weakly exothermic CT-CS offset of about 0.05-0.075 eV; the T-CT3-CS pathway requires the same CT-CS alignment plus a small CT-T offset, no more than about 0.1 eV, corresponding to a recycling factor K greater than about 10^-2, to maintain fast T-to-CT3 recycling. CT-CS alignment is the main determinant of the charge-generation-voltage-loss trade-off, while triplet-recycling kinetics determines whether this balance survives at the device level. This work provides a unified theoretical description from exciton generation to free charge collection, offering a convenient tool for transient and steady-state analysis in organic photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: An exciton-kinetics coupled drift-diffusion model shows that CT-CS energy alignment is the dominant lever controlling the trade-off between charge generation and voltage loss in organic photovoltaics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model gives device designers actionable energy-offset targets for optimizing both photocurrent extraction and open-circuit voltage in singlet/triplet-mediated OPV blends.
method: Self-consistently couples exciton state kinetics with drift-diffusion charge transport.
Solves singlet and triplet populations with reversible photophysical transitions for transient and steady-state response.
Tests how LE-CT, CT-CS, and LE-T offsets plus triplet-transfer rates affect generation, recombination, and voltage loss.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports successful reproduction of triplet-mediated recombination in PM6:Y6 and material-dependent triplet recycling in D18:NFA blends, with design rules derived from the simulations.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted performance is highly sensitive to CT-CS alignment and triplet-recycling kinetics, so inaccurate energetic parameters or temperature dependence could shift the optimal design window.
infographic.paper_title: Device Model Linking Singlet and Triplet Spin-State Properties to Organic Photovoltaic Device Characteristics

title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses
authors: Sinan Genc, Talat Ozden, Alpan Bek
abstract: Coloring building-integrated photovoltaics poses a dilemma: absorptive pigments cost photocurrent, while ordered photonic structures are iridescent. Amorphous photonic glasses, disordered packings of high-index nanospheres, are proposed to avoid both, yet their angle-independent color has rarely been quantified on a realistic module stack. A non-absorbing scatterer needs a high index with visible transparency, which the Moss rule caps near 2.35. Coupling Mie scattering, the Percus-Yevick structure factor, the exact phase function, and two-flux transfer with absorption and refraction at the front glass, we fix four target colors that a crowd-sourced naming survey calls unambiguously blue, green, gold, and terracotta, and map the recipes reaching them across four metal oxides, four encapsulants, two cell technologies, and wide ranges of particle size, packing fraction, and layer number. All four are reached in a laminated three-layer coating, to within DeltaE00 of 0.8 to 2.5, but not from one oxide: transparent TiO2 renders the blue and only pale warm tones; the green, gold, and terracotta require the blue-band absorption of V2O5, and the low-contrast oxides turn grey at the warm end. The encapsulant governs the color, and the cell technology does not. Disorder does not confer angle independence: the colors hold for an observer moving under a fixed sun but drift by DeltaE00 of 5 to 18 over the day, terracotta least, and a facade lit from above and viewed from below shifts every color towards the blue. Oxide, layer number, and facade geometry must therefore be designed together.

infographic.key_insight: Disordered metal-oxide photonic glasses can produce the target building-integrated PV colors without strong iridescence, but the achievable color and its stability depend critically on oxide choice, encapsulant, and facade geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work provides a design map for tuning PV module appearance while preserving transparency constraints, helping engineers co-design color with energy generation in building-integrated photovoltaics.
method: Coupled Mie scattering, Percus–Yevick structure factor, and exact phase-function calculations for disordered nanosphere packings.
Included front-glass refraction and absorption using a two-flux transfer model on realistic laminated module stacks.
Swept oxide type, particle size, packing fraction, layer number, encapsulant, and cell technology to match target colors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors matched four named target colors (blue, green, gold, terracotta) in a three-layer coating with DeltaE00 roughly 0.8–2.5, and quantified viewing-angle/daylight drift of about DeltaE00 5–18.
infographic.watch_item: Angle independence is limited in real use: color can shift substantially over the day and with facade viewing geometry, so optical design must be co-optimized for installation conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses

title: Engineering Correlated Transparent Conductors via Metal-Insulator Transition Proximity
authors: Amit Cohen, Nofar Tuval, Maria Baskin, Tien-Lin Lee, Tom Tiwald, Scott A. Chambers
abstract: Transparent conductors are key functional materials in modern optoelectronic devices. Their performance is governed by an inherent trade-off between optical transparency and electrical conductivity. Correlated metallic oxides offer an attractive workaround to this compromise, where narrow partially-filled bands provide high conductivity, while the absence of visible-range transitions enables optical transparency. Despite this promise, transparency and conductivity remain coupled through carrier density and electronic coherence. Here, we use proximity to a metal-insulator transition (MIT) as a design principle for engineering this balance in correlated-oxide transparent conductors. Epitaxial Ti-substituted $SrVO_3$ films serve as a model platform where the optical window and metallicity are tuned simultaneously. We demonstrate and explain a systematic broadening of the optical window to regimes relevant for silicon photovoltaics. This gain is counterbalanced by carrier depletion and disorder, which drive the loss of coherent transport near the composition-driven MIT. A Haacke figure-of-merit analysis identifies the optimal composition range near the MIT, where the loss of metallic transport is accompanied by persistent near-Fermi-level spectral weight, indicating disorder-assisted localization together with correlation-driven spectral-weight redistribution. These findings establish proximity to an MIT as a general materials-design strategy, using electronic filling as a tuning knob for the transparency-conductivity balance in correlated-oxide transparent conductors.

infographic.key_insight: Proximity to a metal-insulator transition can be used to tune correlated-oxide transparent conductors so they become more transparent without completely sacrificing metallic transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a materials-design rule for optimizing transparent electrodes in optoelectronic and silicon-photovoltaic devices by adjusting electronic filling near the MIT.
method: Use epitaxial Ti-substituted SrVO3 films as a model correlated-oxide transparent conductor.
Systematically vary composition to move toward the metal-insulator transition and track optical window and conductivity together.
Assess performance with Haacke figure-of-merit analysis and spectral-weight measurements near the Fermi level.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a systematic widening of the optical window into silicon-photovoltaic-relevant ranges, with optimal figures of merit found near the composition-driven MIT despite reduced coherent transport.
infographic.watch_item: Near the optimal regime, disorder and carrier depletion can erode coherent conductivity, so implementation must balance transparency gains against transport loss.
infographic.paper_title: Engineering Correlated Transparent Conductors via Metal-Insulator Transition Proximity

title: Wavelength-Dependent Photoluminescence Mapping of Depth-Dependent Degradation Under Thermal Stress in Phenethylammonium Tetrafluoroborate Treated Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Julisa Juarez, Akash Dasgupta, Alan Zhan, Lamtiur P. Samosir, David S. Ginger*
abstract: Studying real-time degradation in perovskite semiconductors remains an important challenge. Conventional methods often cannot separate interfacial and bulk processes or rely on destructive analysis. Here, we demonstrate multiwavelength excitation photoluminescence (PL) as a nondestructive approach to distinguish interface- and bulk-dominated recombination losses. Using phenethylammonium tetrafluoroborate (PEABF4) treatment as a model, we use PL to show that PEABF4 passivates the electron transport layer (ETL)/perovskite interface, reducing interfacial recombination losses from fullerene deposition. However, upon thermal aging, PEABF4-treated stacks degrade more rapidly, with recombination losses broadening from the ETL/perovskite interface into the absorber. Diffusion-recombination simulations support interpreting excitation-wavelength-dependent PL decay signatures consistent with changes in surface recombination velocity and bulk lifetime, providing a framework for depth-sensitive comparisons during aging. Collectively, these results further establish multiwavelength excitation PL as a platform for studying recombination losses during aging of perovskite films.

infographic.key_insight: Multiwavelength photoluminescence can non-destructively distinguish whether degradation in perovskite solar cells starts at the ETL/perovskite interface or spreads into the absorber under heat.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical diagnostic for evaluating passivation strategies like PEABF4 and for tracking depth-resolved stability losses during device aging.
method: Excitation-wavelength-dependent PL mapping to probe different depths nondestructively
Compare fresh vs thermally aged PEABF4-treated and untreated stacks
Use diffusion-recombination simulations to interpret PL decay in terms of surface recombination velocity and bulk lifetime
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that PEABF4 reduces interfacial recombination initially, but thermal aging causes faster PL decay and a broader loss profile extending from the ETL/perovskite interface into the absorber.
infographic.watch_item: PL-based depth interpretation depends on model assumptions and may be sensitive to sample optics, so calibration is needed before generalizing across device architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Wavelength-Dependent Photoluminescence Mapping of Depth-Dependent Degradation Under Thermal Stress in Phenethylammonium Tetrafluoroborate Treated Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion
authors: Robert H. Gordon, Rachel C. Kilbride, Michael Hutton, Jenny Clark, Robert D. J. Oliver
abstract: Solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion offers a compelling route to harvest sub-bandgap photons to increase the efficiency of photovoltaics, but low sensitizer doping required to suppress non-radiative aggregation quenching severely restricts light absorption. Here, we present a dual-resonator planar silver microcavity housing a thermally co-evaporated rubrene:palladium phthalocyanine (PdPC) active layer designed to simultaneously enhance triplet-sensitizer absorption and out-couple upconverted emission. By aligning a dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at $32^\circ$, we achieve a 12-fold enhancement in absorptance at 665 nm. This absorption boost, combined with directional outcoupling through a second cavity mode, outweighs cavity-induced reabsorption losses to yield a 22-fold peak and 4.5-fold integrated enhancement in detected upconversion emission. Overall, this work highlights the potential of microcavity integration to substantially enhance solid-state upconversion performance across low-intensity optoelectronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: A dual-resonator silver microcavity can simultaneously boost sensitizer absorption and directional emission in solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach offers a practical optical-cavity strategy to improve sub-bandgap light harvesting for more efficient photovoltaic and low-intensity optoelectronic devices.
method: Thermally co-evaporated a rubrene:PdPC active layer inside a planar silver microcavity.
Aligned one dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at 32° to enhance sensitizer absorptance.
Used a second cavity mode to out-couple upconverted emission while balancing reabsorption losses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 12-fold absorptance enhancement at 665 nm, a 22-fold peak increase in detected upconversion emission, and a 4.5-fold improvement when integrated over the emission band.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on precise cavity-mode alignment and may be sensitive to reabsorption, aggregation quenching, and fabrication tolerances.
infographic.paper_title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion

title: Tellurium trioxide as an n-type wide-gap semiconductor with ultrahigh work functions from first principles
authors: Tianwei Wang, Teruya Nagafuji, Kota Hanzawa, Hidenori Hiramatsu, Fumiyasu Oba
abstract: The exploration of next-generation wide-gap semiconductors with extreme work functions is highly desirable for the continued advancement of electronic and optoelectronic devices. By using first principles calculations, we show that \b{eta}-TeO3, with a wide band gap exceeding 3 eV, emerges as a promising n-type semiconductor exhibiting ultrahigh work functions of up to ~8 eV. Intentionally or unintentionally incorporated interstitial H, Li, Na, Cu, Mg, and Zn impurities and substitutional F impurities are identified as shallow donors, whereas O vacancies act as minor carrier-compensating defects that locally trap electrons at neighbouring Te sites. The work function is evaluated across a series of low-index nonpolar surfaces. The presence of ordered O vacancies is energetically favoured on these surfaces and tends to reduce the corresponding work functions. These findings underscore the significance of precise control over the O chemical potential to suppress surface O-vacancy formation, thereby preserving the exceptional electronic performance of \b{eta}-TeO3 associated with ultrahigh work functions. Collectively, the results highlight the potential of \b{eta}-TeO3 for hole injection/extraction/transport layers as well as transparent electrodes for applications such as light-emitting devices and photovoltaic cells, while providing useful guidance on carrier doping and surface tuning for these practical applications through elucidating the effects of the point-defect and surface configurations on the electronic properties.

infographic.key_insight: β-TeO3 is predicted from first principles to be a wide-gap n-type semiconductor with exceptionally high work functions, reaching about 8 eV.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes β-TeO3 a strong candidate for hole-transport, hole-injection, and transparent-electrode layers in optoelectronic devices such as solar cells and LEDs.
method: First-principles defect calculations for point impurities and vacancies
Work-function evaluation on low-index nonpolar surfaces
Comparison of defect energetics under different oxygen chemical potentials
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a band gap exceeding 3 eV, shallow-donor behavior for several impurities, and work functions up to ~8 eV depending on surface termination and defect configuration.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may be reduced if oxygen chemical potential is not tightly controlled, since ordered surface O vacancies are favored and can lower the work function.
infographic.paper_title: Tellurium trioxide as an n-type wide-gap semiconductor with ultrahigh work functions from first principles

title: Dynamic Chemical Changes of Ti3C2Tx MXenes in Halide Perovskite Precursor Environments
authors: Kirill Sobolev, Nagaprasad Reddy Samala, Mariela J. Pavan, Sharon Hazan, Vladimir Ezersky, Shakked Schwartz
abstract: The integration of two-dimensional Ti3C2Tx MXenes into Halide Perovskite (HaP) optoelectronics has shown immense potential for enhancing device performance, yet the fundamental chemical interactions within the precursor ink (a critical stage determining the final material state) remain largely unexplored. This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the chemical stability and surface evolution of Ti3C2Tx MXenes when exposed to the individual and combined components of a model methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) solution. By combining detailed X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) analysis with Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, we decouple the complex interactions between MXenes and the ink constituents. We demonstrate that elemental iodine (I2) and polyiodides (In-) act as aggressive oxidizers, triggering rapid degradation and dissolution of the MXene flakes. Conversely, lead iodide (PbI2) induces a slower oxidation process driven by the strong adsorption of Pb2+ ions onto oxygen terminated sites. In stark contrast, methylammonium iodide (MAI) exhibits a stabilizing effect: it adsorbs onto the MXene surface via hydrogen bonding, effectively passivating the flakes and retarding degradation. In addition, our results reveal that the sequence of precursor addition governs the MXene surface state, requiring extra caution, but also enabling further tunability. These findings provide a critical view on how MXene integration with materials, in general, and HaP in particular, should be perceived, providing a fundamental for their rational engineering.

infographic.key_insight: Ti3C2Tx MXenes are chemically unstable in halide perovskite precursor inks, with I2/polyiodides causing rapid degradation, PbI2 causing slower oxidation, and MAI providing surface passivation and stabilization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The order and composition of perovskite precursors can materially change MXene surface chemistry, so ink formulation and mixing sequence must be controlled for reliable device integration.
method: XPS tracked MXene surface composition after exposure to individual and combined MAPbI3 precursor components.
DFT explained the differing adsorption/oxidation pathways for I2, Pb2+, and MAI on Ti3C2Tx surfaces.
Comparative chemical analysis decoupled the roles of each ink constituent in MXene degradation or stabilization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports complementary XPS and DFT results showing rapid I2/polyiodide-driven degradation, slower PbI2-induced oxidation, and MAI-mediated passivation of Ti3C2Tx flakes.
infographic.watch_item: MXene behavior depends on precursor order and environment, so implementation requires careful control of ink mixing sequence to avoid unintended degradation.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Chemical Changes of Ti3C2Tx MXenes in Halide Perovskite Precursor Environments

title: Perspective: The HSE Screened Hybrid and the Band Gap Problem: Origins, Impact, and the Contenders
authors: Gustavo E. Scuseria
abstract: The ideas behind the screened hybrid functional HSE took shape in the early 2000s, about a quarter century ago. HSE was not explicitly designed to predict band gaps, although at the time we did recognize that hybrids could help address the band-gap problem. It was designed to make exact exchange affordable and physically defensible in extended systems. Keeping exact exchange at short range and screening it away at long range inverted the prescription developed for molecules. When HSE band gaps for ordinary semiconductors and selected metal oxides came out substantially closer to experiment than those obtained with conventional semilocal approximations, we were pleasantly surprised and encouraged by the path we had taken. The revision from HSE03 to HSE06 improved molecular thermochemistry while preserving the good accuracy for semiconductor gaps. The one-quarter exchange fraction was inherited unchanged from the successful unscreened PBE hybrid for molecules, rather than fitted to solids. HSE established a practical screened-hybrid approach for accurate band-gap calculations, expanding first-principles work in defect physics, photovoltaics, power electronics, and quantum information, among other areas. The first part of this Perspective recounts the decisions made at HSE's birth and their influence on subsequent developments. The second part assesses recent advances in semilocal and hybrid functionals against benchmarks on sets of solids. Recent meta-GGAs achieve HSE06-level accuracy for selected semiconductors, while dielectric-dependent and tuned hybrids address the limitations of fixed screening. These hybrid developments share with our early work on local hybrids and local range separation the aim of adapting exact exchange to the electronic environment. The comparisons assess band gaps alongside structures, energetics, computational cost, and transferability.

infographic.key_insight: The HSE screened hybrid functional made exact exchange practical for solids and unexpectedly delivered much better band-gap predictions than semilocal DFT, helping establish screened hybrids as a key tool for materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational materials design, HSE and its descendants improve the reliability of band gaps, defect energetics, and screening for semiconductors, oxides, photovoltaics, power electronics, and quantum information materials.
method: Short-range exact exchange + long-range screening to make hybrid DFT feasible for extended systems
Use of a fixed 25% exchange fraction inherited from the PBE0 molecular hybrid
Comparison of HSE and newer semilocal/hybrid functionals against solid-state benchmarks across gaps, structures, and energetics
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that HSE band gaps for ordinary semiconductors and selected metal oxides came out substantially closer to experiment than conventional semilocal approximations, and that recent meta-GGAs can reach HSE06-level accuracy for selected semiconductors.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed screening and a fixed exchange fraction may not transfer uniformly across all materials, so dielectric-dependent or tuned hybrids may be needed for harder cases.
infographic.paper_title: Perspective: The HSE Screened Hybrid and the Band Gap Problem: Origins, Impact, and the Contenders

title: High-throughput computational discovery of CuI-based ternary $p$-type transparent conductors
authors: Michael Seifert, Miguel A. L. Marques, Silvana Botti
abstract: P-type transparent conducting materials (TCMs) remain scarce, limiting progress in transparent electronics and tandem photovoltaics. Here, we perform a high-throughput computational search across CuI-based ternary X--Cu--I compounds using the minima hopping method combined with density functional theory. Filtering for thermodynamic stability, optical transparency, and light hole effective mass, we identify 58 candidate p-type TCMs, of which 49 are previously unreported. Twenty are p-type degenerate semiconductors with intrinsic hole carriers, including Cu$_2$FI$_2$ (calculated gap 3.75 eV, hole effective mass $0.262\,m_0$). We further use this dataset to revisit the chemical modulation of the valence band (CMVB) design rules, originally formulated for Cu-based delafossite oxides. Four generalizations emerge: linear Cu coordination is not required, as tetrahedral coordination (CN = 4) is compatible with p-type TCM character; the mechanism extends to halide-based systems with I $5p$ anion states; the Cu $d$ state energy center $ε_d$ is a quantitative descriptor for valence band dispersion; and Cu undercoordination in monovalent-anion hosts drives intrinsic p-type carrier generation through stoichiometric charge balance. These results establish a generalized computational framework for the design of p-type halide TCMs.

infographic.key_insight: A high-throughput DFT/minima-hopping search identified 58 stable CuI-based ternary compounds with promising p-type transparent conductor behavior, including 20 intrinsically degenerate semiconductors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work expands the design space for transparent electronics and tandem photovoltaics by showing that chemically tunable Cu–I halides can deliver both wide gaps and mobile holes.
method: Minima hopping structure search across X–Cu–I composition space
Density functional theory screening for stability, optical transparency, and hole effective mass
Revisiting CMVB design rules using the discovered compound dataset
infographic.evidence_signal: From the abstract, 58 candidates passed the screening filters, 49 were previously unreported, and Cu2FI2 was highlighted with a 3.75 eV gap and 0.262 m0 hole effective mass.
infographic.watch_item: These are computational predictions, so experimental synthesis, defect control, and carrier mobility verification remain necessary before device adoption.
infographic.paper_title: High-throughput computational discovery of CuI-based ternary $p$-type transparent conductors

title: Mobility-lifetime relation links photodegradation in spin-coated and gravure-printed organic solar cells
authors: Maria Saladina, Paul Weitz, David Holzner, Chen Wang, Robert Eland, Svitlana Taranenko
abstract: The degradation mechanisms of organic solar cells (OSCs) have been studied primarily in spin-coated, laboratory-scale devices, whereas scalable processing modifies the device architecture, active-layer morphology, and underlying charge-transport and recombination properties. Whether these changes also alter how solar cells degrade remains unclear. Here, we compare spin-coated and fully roll-to-roll-compatible gravure-printed PM6:Y12 solar cells during $\sim$1000 h of continuous illumination. Despite distinct initial properties and degradation signatures, the loss of power-conversion efficiency systematically follows the mobility-lifetime product $μτ$. Remarkably, ageing of the printed devices increases the recombination lifetime while strongly reducing charge-carrier mobility, showing that a longer lifetime alone does not imply improved device performance. The mobility reduction is accompanied by decreased PM6 lamellar order, whereas the additional open-circuit voltage loss originates predominantly from increased non-radiative recombination. Dark recovery further reveals a metastable contribution specific to the printed architecture. These results identify the mobility-lifetime product as a unifying physical descriptor for photodegradation, linking ageing-induced microscopic changes to macroscopic performance loss across spin-coated and scalable printed OSCs.

infographic.key_insight: Across both spin-coated and gravure-printed organic solar cells, photodegradation is best unified by the mobility-lifetime product (μτ), not by lifetime alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scalable OSC manufacturing, preserving carrier mobility is as critical as maintaining recombination lifetime, because mobility loss can dominate efficiency decay even when lifetime increases.
method: Compared spin-coated and fully roll-to-roll-compatible gravure-printed PM6:Y12 devices.
Tracked performance and transport parameters during ~1000 h of continuous illumination.
Related degradation signatures to microscopic changes in morphology, recombination, and dark recovery behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: After ~1000 h illumination, efficiency loss tracked the mobility-lifetime product μτ across both device types, with printed devices showing increased lifetime but strongly reduced mobility and added open-circuit-voltage loss from non-radiative recombination.
infographic.watch_item: The printed-architecture-specific metastable recovery indicates that degradation pathways may not transfer directly from lab-scale spin-coated devices to scalable manufacturing without architecture-specific validation.
infographic.paper_title: Mobility-lifetime relation links photodegradation in spin-coated and gravure-printed organic solar cells

title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
authors: Simone Grillo, Offir Zachs Maishlos, Liya Koren, Rotem Strassberg, Rachel Lifer, Edi Maizenberg
abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.

infographic.key_insight: Sb doping in Na/K-alloyed Cs2BInCl6 double perovskite nanocrystals creates self-trapped excitons whose photoluminescence color and polarization anisotropy are strongly composition-dependent, even though absorption stays nearly unchanged.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work shows how B-site alloying can tune emission fingerprints in lead-free perovskites, offering a route to design optoelectronic materials with controllable color, radiative efficiency, and polarization response.
method: Optical spectroscopy of Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals across Na-to-K B-site alloying
Ab initio calculations of excitonic states, lattice distortion, and STE formation
Time-resolved polarization anisotropy measurements to test predicted wavefunction structure
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports PL tuning from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV while absorption near 3.8 eV remains nearly unchanged, and measured anisotropy closely matches theory.
infographic.watch_item: The strong composition dependence appears tied to subtle lattice distortions and STE formation, so device performance may be sensitive to synthesis control and phase/stoichiometry uniformity.
infographic.paper_title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites

title: Computing at the Edge Enabled by Indoor Photovoltaics and Ferroelectrics
authors: Robert L. Z. Hoye, Markus Hellenbrand, Nuno Estrócio, Austin M. Kay, Alice Scardina, Alessandro Mezzetti
abstract: The exponential, pervasive rise of artificial intelligence (AI), hosted in large data centres, will test the limits of the underpinning infrastructure, including electricity and water supplies, which are becoming increasingly precious resources. Rather than performing all AI computations in centralized servers, for many functionalities, these can be performed locally across a network of billions of small, autonomous nodes, saving substantial energy costs associated with communication. This alternative paradigm is known as edge computing, or distributed intelligence (DI), but has been held back by the lack of availability of reliable local energy supplies matching the energy requirements of the computational infrastructure. Opportunities to address this challenge are emerging with rapid advances in high-performance indoor photovoltaics (IPVs) for local energy harvesting, as well as reductions in computational cost through neuromorphic or in-memory computing devices. In this perspective, we discuss the requirements of IPVs for DI, the extent to which emerging materials fulfil these requirements, and how current gaps could be addressed. We make the case that (anti)ferroelectric materials can surpass bottlenecks for both electrostatic energy storage and low-power in-memory neuromorphic computing. The core theme of this perspective is that co-creation between energy harvesting, storage and computing is essential for making DI a reliable and more sustainable alternative to centralized AI.

infographic.key_insight: Indoor photovoltaics, energy storage, and low-power (anti)ferroelectric computing can be co-designed to enable reliable edge AI without relying on centralized data centers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper frames a practical pathway for distributed intelligence by matching local energy harvesting and storage to the power needs of neuromorphic or in-memory computation.
method: Assess the energy requirements of edge/distributed intelligence against available local power supplies.
Evaluate emerging indoor photovoltaic materials for harvesting ambient indoor light efficiently.
Argue that (anti)ferroelectrics can address both electrostatic energy storage and low-power neuromorphic computing bottlenecks.
infographic.evidence_signal: This is a perspective article that synthesizes current material trends and system requirements rather than reporting new experimental benchmarks in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: A key implementation concern is whether real indoor light levels, storage losses, and device reliability can jointly meet the sustained power demands of practical distributed AI nodes.
infographic.paper_title: Computing at the Edge Enabled by Indoor Photovoltaics and Ferroelectrics

title: Disorder-Induced Griffiths like Phase and Charge Localization in Sr2FeRuO6
authors: Koustav Pal, Shuvendu Ghosh, I. Das
abstract: A comprehensive understanding of complex transition-metal oxides is key to designing next-generation spintronic materials with tailored magnetic and transport functionalities. We investigate the interplay among structural disorder, frustrated magnetism, and localized charge transport in the 3d-4d hybrid double perovskite Sr2FeRuO6. The compound adopts a monoclinic structure with significant B-site antisite disorder that drives its unconventional behavior. Magnetic measurements uncover a robust Griffiths phase extending well above the ordering temperature, evidencing stable short-range ferromagnetic clusters within a disordered matrix. Electrical transport remains strongly localized, transitioning from small-polaron hopping at high temperatures to variable-range hopping at intermediate temperatures. These results position Sr2FeRuO6 as a representative 3d-4d hybrid system in which quenched disorder stabilizes spin inhomogeneity, while polaronic and hopping transport are also observed.

infographic.key_insight: Quenched B-site disorder in monoclinic Sr2FeRuO6 stabilizes a Griffiths-like magnetic regime with short-range ferromagnetic clusters and strongly localized charge transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work shows how controlled cation disorder in 3d-4d double perovskites can tune magnetic inhomogeneity and hopping-based transport for spintronic materials design.
method: Structural characterization of the monoclinic, antisite-disordered double perovskite.
Magnetic measurements to identify a robust Griffiths phase above the ordering temperature.
Electrical transport analysis to distinguish small-polaron hopping and variable-range hopping behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports magnetic and transport data showing a Griffiths phase above the transition temperature and a temperature-dependent crossover from small-polaron hopping to variable-range hopping.
infographic.watch_item: Because the behavior is strongly tied to disorder and localization, performance may be sensitive to synthesis quality and antisite concentration.
infographic.paper_title: Disorder-Induced Griffiths like Phase and Charge Localization in Sr2FeRuO6

title: Combined photoluminescence and electrical characterization of valley photovoltaic devices explained with an equivalent circuit
authors: Daixi Xia, Abhinav S. Sharma, Andreas Pusch, Murad J. Y. Tayebjee, Michael P. Nielsen, Fiacre E. Rougieux
abstract: We present an equivalent-circuit analysis that simultaneously considers the photoluminescence and electrical responses of valley photovoltaic devices. Valley photovoltaics (VPV) are a novel concept for hot-carrier solar cells, where intervalley scattering of electrons in the absorbing material helps maintain the conduction-band electron populations at metastable satellite valleys, which are at energies higher than the conduction-band minimum. We measure intensity- and voltage-dependent photoluminescence and electrical signals of a VPV device, which has previously shown S-shaped current-voltage characteristics and thus low efficiency. We present an equivalent circuit that captures the S-shaped current-voltage curves and simultaneously describes our photoluminescence and electric measurements. The equivalent-circuit model indicates that a reverse diode causes inefficient extraction of electrons and thus the S shape. We use a Poisson/drift-diffusion model to demonstrate that the reverse diode can be either explained by the valley-scattering process itself or a heterojunction barrier. The reverse diode must be eliminated before VPV devices can achieve high efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: An equivalent-circuit model shows that the S-shaped voltage response and photoluminescence behavior of the valley photovoltaic device are caused by a reverse diode that impedes electron extraction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work identifies a concrete device-level failure mode in valley photovoltaics, giving designers a clear target for improving carrier extraction and pushing efficiency higher.
method: Measured intensity- and voltage-dependent photoluminescence.
Collected electrical current-voltage characteristics showing S-shaped behavior.
Fit both optical and electrical data with a unified equivalent-circuit model, supported by Poisson/drift-diffusion analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model simultaneously explains the device’s photoluminescence and electrical measurements, including the previously observed S-shaped current-voltage curves.
infographic.watch_item: The reverse-diode effect must be eliminated, and it may arise from either valley-scattering physics or a heterojunction barrier.
infographic.paper_title: Combined photoluminescence and electrical characterization of valley photovoltaic devices explained with an equivalent circuit

title: Computational investigation of a perovskite LaBiO$_{3}$ for photovoltaic, thermoelectric, and optoelectronic applications
authors: M. M. Woldemariam, N. G. Debelo, T. K. Tufa, E. M. Gurmesa, S. H. Didu, S. N. Asfaw
abstract: Using density functional theory (DFT) with the ONCVVPSP pseudopotential and PBE functional, this study investigates the structural, electronic, elastic, optical, and thermoelectric properties of the trigonal LaBiO$_{3}$ perovskite oxide (space group R3c). Ground-state parameters lattice constant, volume, bulk modulus, and its pressure derivative were determined using the equation of state. Applying the Hubbard correction (GGA+U) revealed an indirect, wide band gap of 3.51 eV. Mechanical properties, including the anisotropy factor, elastic modulus, and Poisson's ratio, were calculated via the Voigt-Reuss-Hill averaging scheme. The bulk-to-shear modulus ratio identifies the trigonal phase as ductile. Additionally, Debye temperatures and sound velocities were computed. Optical characteristics (absorption coefficient, refractive index, and electron energy loss function) were evaluated across a 0-35 eV spectral range. Finally, semi-classical transport coefficients, including electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and power factor, were calculated to assess the material's thermoelectric potential.

infographic.key_insight: DFT+U predicts trigonal LaBiO3 is a stable, ductile wide-band-gap semiconductor with promising optical and thermoelectric features for optoelectronic and photovoltaic exploration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The computed electronic, elastic, optical, and transport properties provide a screening basis for assessing LaBiO3 as a functional oxide for solar-energy and device applications.
method: DFT with ONCVVPSP pseudopotentials and PBE exchange-correlation
GGA+U correction to refine the electronic structure and band gap
Voigt-Reuss-Hill averaging plus optical and transport coefficient calculations
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports an indirect band gap of 3.51 eV and evaluates structure, elasticity, optics, and semiclassical transport across a 0–35 eV range.
infographic.watch_item: Results are theoretical and depend on the chosen functional/U value, so experimental validation is needed before device implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Computational investigation of a perovskite LaBiO$_{3}$ for photovoltaic, thermoelectric, and optoelectronic applications
